name: Facelift / neck lift

card.summary: Surgical lifting of the face and neck tissues; the most established anti-aging surgery, with decades of techniques and published complication data.
card.aka: rhytidectomy, deep plane facelift, SMAS lift, platysmaplasty
card.note: Hematoma and nerve injury are the main documented risks; reviews find no single technique clearly superior.

quick.overview:
A facelift (rhytidectomy) repositions and tightens facial tissues and usually removes excess skin to give a more youthful contour, and a neck lift addresses the jawline and neck, often by treating the platysma muscle. They are often combined.

In looksmaxxing forums, facelifts are discussed mainly as older-man anti-aging surgery and as a one-time investment, with arguments over whether to choose surgery or fillers. A review of facelift controversies concluded that the available techniques are generally equal in efficacy.
quick.mechanism: Techniques range from skin-only lifts to SMAS and deep plane lifts that reposition deeper layers, with neck work such as platysma plication or submental liposuction. Recent literature emphasises restoring volume and lifting vertically rather than pulling the skin sideways.
quick.risks: Documented complications include hematoma (the most common), nerve injury, skin necrosis (higher in smokers), scarring, hair loss at incisions and ear position changes. Wikipedia reports the ideal age for a facelift, by patient satisfaction, as 50 or younger, and cites typical skin-only results lasting 5 to 10 years.

lead: A facelift, or rhytidectomy, is cosmetic surgery that makes the lower and mid face look younger: it repositions sagging tissue, removes excess skin and redrapes what remains over the face and neck. For appearance it targets the features that age shifts most visibly, namely jowls, deepened nasolabial folds, a softened jawline and loose neck skin, so that the jaw-to-neck line looks tighter and more defined.[1][18] It is often combined with eyelid surgery, fat grafting and a neck lift.

A neck lift (platysmaplasty) addresses the area under the chin and along the neck: surgeons tighten or reposition the platysma muscle, remove or reshape fat and trim skin, which sharpens the cervicomental angle that people often call the jawline-neck transition.[19][20] Facelift and neck lift are frequently performed together, and in looksmaxxing forums the neck lift is also discussed as a stand-alone option for submental laxity.[4][17]

Facelift techniques have evolved through cutaneous, SMAS, deep plane and volumetric periods since the early 1900s.[1][18] A review of facelift controversies concluded that the available techniques are generally equal in efficacy and called for higher-quality research with standardized outcome assessment.[2] A review of 11,300 facelift patients in a prospective database reported an overall major complication rate of 1.8 percent.[12]

In looksmaxxing communities, facelifts and mini neck lifts are discussed by older men, by people who have lost a lot of weight and by people planning jaw surgery or fat grafting, usually as complements rather than substitutes.[3][4][17]

paras: Rhytidectomy is performed under general anesthesia or deep twilight sleep, and typically removes excess facial skin, with or without tightening of deeper tissues, before redraping the skin.[18] Surgeons describe facial aging in terms of jowls from descent of the platysma, deeper nasolabial folds from descent of cheek fat, and changes in the lower eyelid, with skin quality as a fourth factor.[18] Wikipedia reports that, judged by patient satisfaction, the ideal age is 50 or younger.[18]

The neck lift is a separate but related operation. Platysmaplasty tightens, repositions or supports the platysma muscle, and may include submental liposuction, removal of fat beneath the muscle, and skin excision; because neck aging affects several layers differently, the surgery is individualized.[19][20] Incisions are typically under the chin and/or behind the ears.[19]

Wikipedia attributes the first facelift to Eugen Holländer in Berlin in 1901, and Charles Miller of Chicago wrote the first facial cosmetic surgery textbook in 1907.[18] During World War I, Johannes Esser developed the skin graft inlay technique, which Harold Gillies used, and Dr. Passot published one of the first facelift papers in 1919.[18] Suzanne Noël, described as the first female plastic surgeon, helped develop the field.[18] Early operations pulled the skin and cut away the excess.[18]

Tord Skoog introduced subfacial dissection in 1968 and published it in 1974. In 1976 Mitz and Peyronie described the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS), the fibromuscular layer that surgeons began to tighten separately from the skin.[18]

Paul Tessier used subperiosteal dissection through a coronal incision and in 1979 showed better results than classic lifts.[18] Hamra described the composite rhytidectomy in 1992, a modification of deep-plane surgery that lifts skin, SMAS and orbicularis oculi together.[18]

Surgeons since 1991 have focused on smaller scars, restoring lost volume, and lifting in a cranial rather than posterior direction.[18] Endoscopic approaches were reported in the 1990s, for example a 1994 report of an endoscopic full facelift using total subperiosteal dissection for patients up to their late 40s without skin excision.[21]

A secondary summary lists a 1928 submental approach to the platysma by Julien Bourguet, platysma-fascial rhytidectomy by J. Owsley in 1977, introduction of liposuction to the neck by E. H. Courtiss in 1985, and corset platysmaplasty developed by D. R. Feldman in 1990.[19]

Wikipedia lists SMAS plication (folding the SMAS with less dissection), SMAS flap, deep-plane (lifting skin and soft tissue as a unit by releasing retaining ligaments, more demanding because of nearby facial nerve branches), composite, mid-face, mini (S-lift), subperiosteal, skin-only, thread-lift and MACS approaches.[18] The MACS lift (Minimal Access Cranial Suspension) uses a short incision in front of the ear and is described as taking about 2.5 hours versus 3.5 for traditional lifts, with 2 to 3 weeks of recovery versus 3 to 4.[18]

Authors have described a lateral SMASectomy as a safe, versatile and reproducible technique producing a powerful lift with results similar to a traditional SMAS flap, without the additional risk of nerve injury.[5] Mid-face lifts use small hairline and intraoral incisions and suit people in their 40s with flattened midfaces and little jowling; mini-facelifts omit neck work and use shorter incisions.[18]

For the neck, a vertical neck lifting approach is described as an extended deep plane facelift that redrapes laxity vertically onto the face, with indications for combining it with submental surgery.[6] Medial (corset) platysmaplasty brings the muscle borders together in the midline; lateral platysmapexy supports the muscle laterally; a cited study found medial repair generally more effective than lateral pulling alone for midline deformity.[20] Deep neck techniques address subplatysmal fat, the digastric muscle or the submandibular glands, and excessive fat removal can cause a hollowed 'cobra neck' deformity.[20]

A prospective study of complete platysma transection in 150 consecutive neck-lift patients operated on by one surgeon (2010 to 2014) reported 100 percent satisfaction at 3 months falling to 76 percent at 1 year, with 55 percent free of band recurrence at 1 year; the authors cited long operating time and poor long-term maintenance and called for reconsidering the procedure.[7]

A review of the male facelift notes that men seek a somewhat different outcome and that techniques have been adapted to preserve a masculine appearance free of signs that surgery has been performed.[8] Wikipedia notes that men's hair-bearing preauricular skin and sideburns make a natural result harder to achieve.[18]

A review of facelift controversies found the options generally equal in efficacy and noted the need for standardized preoperative assessment and outcome evaluation.[2] A systematic review of patient-reported outcome measures after facial cosmetic surgery and nonsurgical rejuvenation identified 47 instruments in 442 articles, of which nine met inclusion criteria and none met every development and validation guideline, and its authors called for a new measure reflecting patient perspectives.[9] A pilot study tested four outcome instruments (including a facelift outcomes evaluation) in 78 patients across three private cosmetic surgery centers.[11]

A secondary summary reports a 2017 observer study in which patients looked about 3.7 years younger after facelifts.[10] Wikipedia states a skin-only facelift can last 5 to 10 years, with touch-ups sometimes needed at 6 to 12 months; a secondary summary gives results of 10 to 15 years (range 5 to 15) for neck lifts and about 1 to 2 years for thread lifts.[1][10][19] These longevity figures are secondary-source summaries and vary by technique, age and skin.

Human evidence includes outcome-measure studies, surgeon case series and large complication analyses. A pilot study tested instruments for measuring cosmetic facial plastic surgery outcomes in 78 patients, and an analysis of 11,300 patients from a prospective database (2008 to 2013) found an overall major-complication rate of 1.8 percent, with hematoma the most common at 1.1 percent and infection at 0.3 percent; combined procedures had a higher rate (3.7 percent) than facelift alone (1.5 percent), and male sex predicted hematoma.[11][12]

Registered trials include a comparison of an office-based limited facelift with a hospital full facelift (n=100), a thread lift using retaining ligaments (n=369), and a study of intravenous tranexamic acid during rhytidectomy.[13][14][15] A non-surgical radiofrequency 'facelift' clinical study treated 20 areas in 17 patients.[16]

Wikipedia lists hematoma as the most common complication, with nearly all cases within 24 hours and usually requiring return to the operating room; nerve injury (the greater auricular nerve is the most commonly injured sensory nerve and the facial nerve the most commonly injured motor nerve); skin necrosis with about a 12-fold higher risk in smokers; hypertrophic scarring; permanent temporal hair loss or hairline distortion; ear position changes of up to 1 cm; rare infection; and a 'windswept' look from excessive skin removal or a poor lift vector.[18] Smoking, hypertension and diabetes raise complication risk, and patients are usually told to stop aspirin or blood thinners at least one week beforehand.[18]

A secondary summary puts neck-lift hematoma at about 1 to 5 percent and notes rarer nerve injury, skin necrosis, deep vein thrombosis and results needing revision.[19] Wikipedia warns that thread lifts have been associated with serious complications and inadequate UK training.[18]

In 2019 the facelift was the third most popular aesthetic surgery after rhinoplasty and blepharoplasty according to the American Society for Aesthetic Plastic Surgery data cited on Wikipedia. Costs as of 2008 ranged from US$2,500 in India and Panama to US$15,000 in the US and Canada, and mostly 4,000 to 9,000 pounds in Europe as of 2009.[18]

A looksmax.org post argues for saving about 15,000 dollars for a single limited facelift in a man's 40s or 50s, and says fillers can leave a face puffy; a reply disagreed that a facelift can only be done once and said results depend on the surgeon.[3]

Other members ask whether a neck lift before jaw surgery would address submental fullness, or whether a mini neck lift would help loose skin after weight loss; one reply says maxillomandibular advancement stretches the suprahyoid muscles and skin to sharpen the submental area.[4][17]

lore.intro: Facelifts appear on looksmax.org in anti-aging threads and as add-ons for jaw and submental concerns.[3][4][17]

claims.claim: A facelift can only be done once or it looks odd
claims.believers: The original post says a limited facelift should be done once, in a man's 40s or 50s.[3]
claims.experts: A reply in the thread says facelifts can be repeated depending on the surgeon.[3] Wikipedia notes that skin-only lifts can need touch-ups at 6 to 12 months.[18]

claims.claim: Surgery beats fillers for keeping a lean face
claims.believers: The post says fillers can make the face look puffy or bloated and that a facelift preserves leanness.[3]
claims.experts: Reviews describe facelift as repositioning tissue, and nonsurgical alternatives as a separate category; no head-to-head comparison is cited here.[1][2]

claims.claim: Jaw advancement surgery improves the submental area
claims.believers: A forum reply says maxillomandibular advancement stretches suprahyoid muscles and skin for a sharper submental area.[4]
claims.experts: No study of that effect is cited here; neck lift technique reviews describe submental contour work as platysma, fat and skin management.[20]

claims.claim: A mini neck lift can fix loose skin under the chin after weight loss
claims.believers: Members who have lost weight or have stubborn submental fat ask about a mini neck lift alongside fat grafting.[17]
claims.experts: A secondary summary describes mini neck lifts as using smaller incisions for milder cases.[19]

claims.claim: A facelift buys 5 to 10 more years of looking younger
claims.believers: The looksmax.org post estimates a limited facelift buys another 5 to 10 years.[3]
claims.experts: A summarized 2017 observer study reported patients looked about 3.7 years younger; Wikipedia gives skin-only durability of 5 to 10 years.[1][10]

claims.claim: Newer deep-plane techniques give better results than older lifts
claims.believers: Technique advocates describe deep-plane and vertical neck lifting as lifting tissue as a unit and releasing ligaments.[6][18]
claims.experts: A review of controversies concluded the literature suggests techniques are generally equal in efficacy.[2]

angle.text: A facelift repositions the cheek, jowl and neck tissues that have descended with age, and a neck lift tightens the platysma and removes excess skin under the chin. Patients and surgeons use the combination to restore a cleaner jaw and neck contour.
